title: Segmentation: per-tile 2-high DRAM micro-stacks bonded over compute
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation, resolving 'more bandwidth vs. limited die-edge shoreline': replace 6-8 edge-mounted 12-high HBM stacks with ~64 two-high DRAM micro-stacks hybrid-bonded on top of each compute tile at ~9 um pitch. Each micro-stack feeds only the tile beneath it, and the logic NoC handles sharing.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and HBM TSV tax (fact 6): wire length drops from ~5 mm to <0.1 mm, so ~3.5 falls to ~0.3 pJ/bit. 2-high stacks avoid compound 12-high yield loss, and shoreline stops limiting bandwidth.

title: Taking out: periphery moved to a bitline-pitch bonded logic wafer
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out the harmful part: the DRAM wafer keeps only cell mats and bitlines. Sense amps, decoders, refresh logic and the HBM PHY sit on a logic-process wafer hybrid-bonded at ~0.7 um pitch, one bond per bitline pair, so data goes from cell to PHY without crossing a slow DRAM-process wire.
why: Periphery (~49% of the die, fact 7) is recovered for cells, giving ~1.7x bits per DRAM wafer. Logic-speed sense amps and wires cut on-die movement energy ~40% and let VARY drop.

title: Local quality: tapered TSV stacks, fewer TSVs in each higher tier
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality: in a uniform HBM stack every die carries the full TSV farm, though the top die needs none. One common front-side mask lays out the TSV farm region as spare subarrays, and a cheap i-line backside mask per tier etches only the TSVs that die needs for the dies above it. In upper tiers the unetched subarrays are fused on as extra capacity.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): average TSV area per die drops ~45% in a 12-high stack, for ~5-10% more bits per stack with the same front-side masks.

title: Asymmetry: read-wide, write-narrow memory links for inference
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: inference reads weights and KV cache 10-50x more than it writes. So ~90% of HBM data lanes become one-way DRAM-to-GPU lanes with open-drain low-swing drivers and receiver-only GPU ends, and a narrow bidirectional lane group handles writes and commands.
why: Data movement (fact 5): read lanes need no ODT or driver pairs and have no turnaround, so PHY energy and area per read bit fall ~25-35% and usable bandwidth rises ~10%.

title: Merging: data carriers superimposed on power TSVs
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging: about half of HBM TSVs carry only VDD/VSS. Superimpose low-amplitude 10-20 GHz on-off-keyed carriers on them, with on-die LC band-pass taps and notch filters on the decoupling network, so power TSVs also carry data without new holes.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): +30-50% bandwidth per unit of TSV area, or ~25% fewer TSVs for the same bandwidth.

title: Universality: coaxial TSV acting as signal, decap and heat pipe
idea: TRIZ #6 Universality: build each signal TSV as a coax with a Cu core, a 20 nm high-k ZrO2 liner and a grounded Cu sleeve. The shielded core carries data at tight pitch, the sleeve-to-substrate stack acts as distributed decoupling capacitance, and the extra copper conducts heat up the stack.
why: HBM TSV tax and power integrity (fact 6): 2x tighter TSV pitch without crosstalk, and no separate decap or dummy thermal TSVs, for a ~20-30% smaller TSV region.

title: Nesting: DRAM dies set into pockets in the GPU backside
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: with backside power delivery the GPU substrate is thinned anyway. Etch ~30 um pockets into its backside and set thinned DRAM dies inside, wired through nano-TSVs into the backside network, so each DRAM die sits ~30 um from the logic it feeds.
why: Data movement (fact 5): the interposer and long wires disappear, for <0.3 pJ/bit and no shoreline limit, and capacity grows with no added footprint.

title: Anti-weight: microfluidic cooling interlayer lifting heat between compute and DRAM
idea: TRIZ #8 Anti-weight (counter a harmful load with a force from the environment): put a 100 um silicon interlayer between a hot accelerator and the DRAM stacked on it. The interlayer has through-vias and two-phase dielectric coolant microchannels that carry compute heat sideways, keeping the DRAM below 85 C.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and refresh (fact 3): memory-on-logic stacking (~10x lower pJ/bit than HBM) becomes possible without the 2x refresh rate required above 85 C.

title: Prior counteraction: counter-bowed dies for 24-high stacks
idea: TRIZ #9 Preliminary anti-action: measure each tier's bonding warpage, then deposit a tuned SiN backside stress film so each thinned die is pre-bowed the opposite way and goes flat at bonding temperature. This removes edge voids in hybrid-bonded 16-24-high stacks.
why: HBM yield (fact 6): aims to recover ~10 of the 20-30 lost yield points and enables 24-high stacks (+50% GB per footprint).

title: Prior action: base-die gather engine packs sparse reads before PHY
idea: TRIZ #10 Preliminary action: the HBM base die runs a scatter-gather and transpose engine. The GPU sends index lists (KV-cache page tables, embedding IDs, MoE token routes), and the base die collects 32 B sectors across banks and packs them into dense full-width bursts before they cross the PHY.
why: Overfetch (fact 8) and data movement (fact 5): 2-8x fewer wasted bits cross the interface on sparse access, and effective bandwidth rises by the same factor.

title: Beforehand cushioning: reusable sacrificial test tier for known-good stacks
idea: TRIZ #11 Beforehand cushioning: after each bonding step, attach a reusable probe die with dense test circuits to the top of the partial stack, using micro-spring contacts and a low-temperature debondable adhesive. It tests every tier and TSV so bad partial stacks are reworked or dropped before more good dies go on, then it is lifted off and reused.
why: HBM yield (fact 6): good dies are no longer stacked onto bad partial stacks, so stack yield rises from ~70% to ~90% and effective HBM cost per GB falls ~20%.

title: Equipotentiality: constant-voltage current-mode TSV signaling
idea: TRIZ #12 Equipotentiality (avoid raising and lowering): a low-impedance common-gate receiver holds each TSV at a fixed mid-rail voltage, and data is sent as the direction of a ~50 uA current. The TSV and microbump capacitance never charges or discharges.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and voltage floor (fact 10): IO energy no longer scales with CV^2, for ~3-5x lower pJ/bit on capacitive vertical links.

title: The other way round: DRAM pushes a precompiled tensor schedule
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way round: instead of the GPU requesting every line, the compiler loads a tensor-streaming schedule into the HBM base die. The base die opens rows in a fixed order and pushes data to the accelerator, so the command/address bus becomes a rarely used control channel.
why: Data movement (fact 5), overfetch (fact 8) and row hammer (fact 9): no request traffic, no row misses, and each row opens once per pass, for ~20-30% more effective bandwidth and fewer activates.

title: Spheroidality: ring of compute chiplets with memory inside and outside
idea: TRIZ #14 Spheroidality (curves instead of lines): place compute chiplets in a ring on a large panel substrate, giving the ring both an inner and an outer shoreline. Memory stacks sit inside the hole and around the outside.
why: Data movement (fact 5): ~1.6x more memory beachfront per unit of compute area at the same short wire length, avoiding longer links with higher pJ/bit.

title: Dynamics: beam-steered free-space optical links between chiplets
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics (make a fixed part adjustable): memory chiplets carry VCSEL arrays and compute chiplets carry photodiode arrays. A lid with a MEMS micromirror or liquid-crystal metasurface re-steers the beams, so any memory chiplet can be pointed at any compute tile for each workload phase.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and pooling: ~0.5-1 pJ/bit over cm distances with no interposer wiring, and idle memory is reassigned instead of over-provisioned.

title: Excessive action: 65,536-bit ultra-wide, ultra-slow hybrid-bonded bus
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial or excessive action: make the bus 32x wider than HBM3 using 3 um hybrid-bond pitch, but run each pin at only 200-400 Mb/s with unterminated 0.4 V inverter drivers and no SerDes, DLL or training.
why: Data movement (fact 5): ~0.05-0.1 pJ/bit IO at HBM3E-class bandwidth, and the PHY shrinks because its circuits are trivial.

title: Another dimension: DRAM dies standing on edge, bonded at sidewalls
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: stand thinned DRAM dies upright like books on a logic base die. Route metal lines to the diced edge and open them as sidewall pads, then solder or hybrid-bond each die's edge to the base, so there are no TSVs and every die has its own path down.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no TSV area and no 12-hop stacking yield cascade, attacking the ~3x area-per-bit penalty, and heat leaves along each die's full height.

title: Mechanical vibration: GHz acoustic links replacing signal TSVs
idea: TRIZ #18 Mechanical vibration: ScAlN thin-film transducers on each die send 5-10 GHz bulk acoustic pulses through the stacked silicon. Each tier's receiver resonates at its own frequency, so tiers are addressed by acoustic frequency instead of by TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): signals need no TSV keep-out or bond alignment, and contactless tiers can be tested and stacked at higher yield.

title: Periodic action: resonant LC-tank data bus recycling switching energy
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: make each wide-bus line part of an LC tank with an inductor in the interposer, so the line rings sinusoidally at the clock rate and data is encoded by conditional phase injection. Energy swings between L and C instead of being dumped on every toggle.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and voltage floor (fact 10): 3-5x lower IO energy on capacitive 1-2k-bit buses.

title: Continuity of useful action: full-duplex simultaneous bidirectional TSVs
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: add hybrid echo-cancelling receivers to every DQ TSV so reads and writes flow on the same wire at the same time. This removes read-write turnaround bubbles and the idle direction.
why: Data movement and HBM TSV tax (facts 5, 6): recovers the 10-20% lost to turnaround and gives up to 2x bandwidth per TSV, so half the DQ TSVs deliver the same bandwidth.

title: Skipping: DRAM dies overhang compute edge, bonded face-to-face, no interposer
idea: TRIZ #21 Skipping (rush through the harmful stage): skip the interposer by bonding each DRAM die face-to-face onto a 1.5 mm strip along the compute die edge. The rest of the DRAM die is cantilevered over a mold shelf that carries its power vias.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and the CoWoS capacity chokepoint: no interposer and no data TSVs, for ~0.3 pJ/bit links.

title: Blessing in disguise: crosstalk-coded TSV arrays using coupling as signal
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise: instead of shielding densely packed TSVs, group them in sets of 4-6 and send chordal vector codes (ENRZ-style). Common-mode coupling cancels while the coupled differential modes carry data, so crosstalk becomes part of the signaling.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): 2x denser TSV pitch at ~1.3-1.5 bits per wire, for ~40% less TSV area per bit.

title: Feedback: self-tuning shared dictionaries compress traffic on both link ends
idea: TRIZ #23 Feedback: the memory base die and the accelerator each keep matched 256-entry value dictionaries. Repeated words (zeros, common weight and activation values) travel as 8-bit indices, and both sides update their dictionaries in lockstep each epoch using hit-rate feedback.
why: Data movement (fact 5): 1.5-3x fewer link bits per useful bit for AI tensors, cutting pJ per useful bit and bandwidth demand.

title: Segmentation: legacy LPDDR4 dies tiled into an HBM-emulator package
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation: instead of one tall TSV stack, tile 24-32 known-good LPDDR4/DDR4 dies from mature 1x/2x-nm DRAM lines flat on a fan-out RDL substrate from existing OSAT lines. Each die gets its own x16 channel, and a 28 nm hub die aggregates them into a 1024-bit HBM-like port. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Capital and HBM tax (facts 4, 6): no TSVs, no hybrid bonders and no leading-edge DRAM wafers. Gives ~50-60% of HBM3 bandwidth at ~40% of HBM cost per GB from idle trailing capacity.

title: Taking out: cold MoE experts moved to router-ahead prefetched DDR4 tier
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out the cold mass: mixture-of-experts models keep only routed-hot experts in HBM, and the rest live in commodity DDR4 behind 28 nm CXL controllers. A tiny predictor runs the next layer's router one layer early so the needed experts stream over CXL before they are used. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Do DRAM's job with less HBM: 2-4x less HBM per accelerator for MoE inference, shifting capacity to cheap trailing-node DRAM.

title: Local quality: LCD-line glass interposers with zoned fine-line RDL
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality: run idle Gen-4/5 LCD TFT lines (1.5-3 um lithography on 730x920 mm glass) to make multilayer Cu RDL glass interposers. Fine lines go only in the memory-to-compute shoreline zones and coarse power planes everywhere else, and a-Si/IGZO TFT switches are built in as lane-repair multiplexers. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Capital and the CoWoS interposer chokepoint: ~10x more area per pass than a 300 mm wafer and ~3-5x lower interposer cost per mm2, and lane repair raises assembly yield.

title: Asymmetry: read-mostly weight tier on legacy NAND with wide parallel reads
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: model weights are written once and read billions of times, so store them in a tier built on 64-layer-era NAND lines. A 28 nm controller reads thousands of planes in parallel, streaming each layer ahead into a small DRAM staging buffer to hide ~30 us read latency, while writes stay slow and rare. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Do DRAM's job with less DRAM: moving weights out of HBM/DRAM frees 30-70% of memory for KV cache, at NAND cost per bit (~1/10 of DRAM) from depreciated lines.

title: Merging: content-addressed CXL appliance deduplicates shared KV prefixes
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging identical objects: a 28 nm CXL memory appliance hashes every 4 KB page written by many inference sessions (shared system prompts, common prefixes, replicated weights). It stores each distinct page once in commodity DDR4 and uses copy-on-write when a page diverges. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Do DRAM's job with less: 2-5x effective capacity for multi-tenant LLM serving with shared prompts, built entirely from trailing-node logic and legacy DRAM.

title: Nesting: legacy DRAM dies embedded inside the organic substrate under the GPU
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: use existing embedded-component substrate lines (already used for power modules and phone substrates) to bury thinned LPDDR/DDR4 dies inside the organic package core directly beneath the accelerator. The dies connect upward through ~100 um laser vias. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Data movement (fact 5) and capacity: adds 16-64 GB per package without shoreline or an interposer, at ~1-2 pJ/bit versus ~10-20 pJ/bit for DDR5 DIMMs.

title: Prior counteraction: pre-emphasis lets HBM-class links run on organic substrate
idea: TRIZ #9 Preliminary anti-action: put feed-forward equalization and per-lane deskew in a 28 nm base/hub die that pre-distorts signals against the known channel loss. This allows 1024-bit memory links on ordinary 2/2 um organic fan-out substrates instead of silicon interposers. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Capital and the CoWoS chokepoint: no silicon interposer for HBM-class memory, ~30-50% lower packaging cost and existing OSAT capacity, at ~1 pJ/bit.

title: Prior action: weights stored entropy-coded, decoded by 28 nm ingress engines
idea: TRIZ #10 Preliminary action: compress model weights offline with per-tensor entropy coding (Huffman/ANS on quantized values) and keep them compressed in DRAM. A 28 nm decoder chiplet at the accelerator's memory ingress expands them at line rate. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Capacity and data movement (fact 5): 1.4-2x fewer DRAM bits and link bits per weight, with the decode logic built in trailing fabs.

title: The other way round: 28 nm attention engines beside DDR4 do decode
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way round: instead of moving the KV cache to the GPU, move the low-arithmetic-intensity attention step to the memory. Memory-rich nodes pair many DDR4 channels with 28 nm attention ASICs that run decode attention in place and return only small output vectors, while the GPU keeps the dense matmuls. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Data movement and HBM demand (facts 5, 6): the KV cache leaves HBM entirely, and only ~1/1000 of the KV bytes cross the network per token.

title: Spheroidality: radial server board with memory cards as equal spokes
idea: TRIZ #14 Spheroidality: lay out a round motherboard with the CPU or accelerator at the center and memory cards plugged in radially like spokes. Every channel gets the same short trace length, so more DIMMs fit per channel at full speed. Built with existing PCB and connector lines. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Capacity per socket and signal integrity (fact 5): ~1.5-2x more DIMMs per socket at DDR5 speed (2 DIMMs per channel without derating), using cheap commodity DIMMs.

title: Dynamics: optical circuit-switched rack memory pool from 90 nm photonics
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics: build memory-pooling links with silicon photonics from existing 90/45 nm photonics foundry lines, plus a MEMS optical circuit switch that reconnects DRAM sleds to whichever servers need them every few seconds. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Do DRAM's job with less: datacenter DRAM utilization rises from ~50% to ~75-80%, so ~30% less DRAM is bought, and optics keep added latency to ~150 ns across racks.

title: Periodic action: follow-the-sun scheduling of memory-heavy jobs
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: memory sits idle on a daily cycle. A global scheduler moves memory-hungry batch jobs (fine-tuning, embedding builds, KV-heavy batch inference) to regions during their off-peak hours and leases out idle DRAM pools through CXL-attached capacity APIs. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Usable supply: 15-25% more useful DRAM-hours from the installed base without any new chips.

title: Continuity: wide-IO DRAM redesigned for fully depreciated legacy DRAM lines
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: keep retiring 2x/3x-nm DRAM lines running by taping out a new 512-bit-wide, low-speed DRAM die for them, designed for fan-out packaging beside accelerators. The wide, slow interface hides the older node's lower density. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Capital (fact 4): depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost, so fully depreciated lines make bits at about half the wafer cost, adding supply with zero new fab capex.

title: Parameter change: chilled DRAM zones cut refresh bandwidth theft
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter changes: give DRAM its own 10-20 C coolant loop on a cold plate separate from the 60 C compute loop, built from existing chiller hardware. Retention roughly doubles for every ~10 C drop, so the refresh interval can stretch 4-8x through standard temperature-controlled refresh modes. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Refresh (fact 3): bandwidth lost to refresh falls from 10-20% to ~2-4%, and refresh energy (16-33% of idle power) falls ~4x, giving more usable bandwidth from the same chips.

title: Copying: passive optical splitters broadcast one weight read to many chips
idea: TRIZ #26 Copying: in data-parallel inference every accelerator holds an identical copy of the weights. Instead, one memory node reads each weight block once and broadcasts it in lockstep to all accelerators through cheap passive 1:16 PON fiber splitters (mass-produced telecom parts). (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Do DRAM's job with less: replicated weight storage falls by up to 16x, freeing HBM for KV cache, using existing telecom optics capacity.

title: Cheap short-living objects: retired server DDR4 reborn as CXL memory
idea: TRIZ #27 Cheap short-living objects: hyperscalers retire millions of DDR4 DIMMs. Collect, retest and bin them, then mount 8-16 on each CXL Type-3 card built around a 28 nm controller, as a cheap cold tier for KV cache and page cache. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Usable supply: reuses DRAM that already exists, at ~10-20% of new DRAM cost per GB and zero wafer starts.

title: Mechanics substitution: polymer optical waveguides replace copper memory traces
idea: TRIZ #28 Mechanics substitution (replace the copper field with light): laminate siloxane polymer waveguides into ordinary PCBs on existing PCB lines, and put 28 nm VCSEL driver chips at the memory controller and on the modules, so memory channels run optically across the board. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Data movement (fact 5): longer reach without retimers lets one socket fan out to many more DIMMs, at ~3-5 pJ/bit versus 10-20 pJ/bit for long copper.

title: Hydraulics: liquid-metal micro-well sockets for reworkable memory chiplets
idea: TRIZ #29 Pneumatics and hydraulics: replace solder microbumps with micro-wells filled with Ga-In liquid metal at ~40 um pitch on the substrate. Memory chiplets press in and are tested in place, and a failed one can be pulled out and replaced. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: HBM yield (fact 6): a bad memory chiplet no longer scraps the whole package, for ~10-20% fewer scrapped multi-thousand-dollar packages using existing OSAT tooling.

title: Thin films: chip-on-film display lines make flexible memory ribbons
idea: TRIZ #30 Flexible shells and thin films: reuse display-driver chip-on-film lines (~18 um pitch on polyimide) to make flexible memory ribbons. LPDDR dies on flex tape are bonded to the package edge and folded up around the cold plate, adding capacity in 3D without using board area. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Capacity per package and data movement (fact 5): ~2x more LPDDR per accelerator at ~2-4 pJ/bit, using idle COF capacity.

title: Color change: wavelength-addressed memory modules on passive AWG routers
idea: TRIZ #32 Color changes: give each memory module its own wavelength. The controller picks a module by tuning its laser color, and a passive arrayed-waveguide grating routes the light, so there is no electrical or optical switch in the path. All parts come from trailing-node photonics and InP laser lines. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Data movement and pooling (fact 5): a switchless memory fabric at ~1-2 pJ/bit over meters, with more modules per controller than copper allows.

title: Homogeneity: maskless direct-write silicon interposers in 200 mm fabs
idea: TRIZ #33 Homogeneity: make interposers from silicon, which matches the dies' CTE, in idle 200 mm fabs, and pattern 2 um Cu RDL with maskless laser direct-imaging tools borrowed from the PCB industry. Interposers can then exceed the reticle limit without stitching and need no masks. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Capital, masks and the CoWoS chokepoint (fact 4): zero mask cost, and larger-than-reticle interposers fit more memory stacks, using depreciated 200 mm capacity.

title: Discarding and recovering: partial-good HBM stacks sold as lower tiers
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: instead of scrapping stacks with one bad tier or weak TSV lanes, fuse out the bad tier or half the lanes in the base die and re-bin the stacks as 8-high or half-width parts for inference cards and edge devices. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: HBM yield (fact 6): turns the 20-30% yield loss into a sellable lower tier, effectively +10-20% usable HBM supply from the same wafers.

title: Phase transition: transient-liquid-phase bonding stacks DRAM in standard reflow
idea: TRIZ #36 Phase transitions: replace scarce hybrid bonders with Cu-Sn transient-liquid-phase bonding in existing OSAT reflow and thermocompression tools. A thin Sn layer melts and converts to high-melting Cu3Sn, so later tiers bond at ~20 um pitch without remelting earlier ones. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Capital and the tool chokepoint (fact 6): 12-16-high stacks without new hybrid-bonding capacity, at finer pitch than standard microbumps.
